analysis.one_liner: Strips pharmacy middlemen of price-spread profits and forces them to charge Medicare flat fees and disclose their dealings.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee approved the bill in December 2023 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that drug plans hire to negotiate prices and pay pharmacies. This bill would stop PBMs in Medicare from taking income from anything but flat, fair-market service fees — no hidden manufacturer rebates kept for themselves, no price-based fees — and require detailed annual reports on what they retain. In Medicaid, it would ban spread pricing, where a middleman charges the state more than it pays the pharmacy and keeps the difference. It would also require PBMs and plans to reveal to pharmacies how claims are priced, replace opaque pharmacy scoring systems with standardized performance measures, curb plans from steering seniors to PBM-owned pharmacies, and commission a series of government studies on drug supply-chain markups.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors in Medicare drug plans and Medicaid enrollees, whose plans would no longer pay middlemen fees that rise with drug prices, and community pharmacies, which currently bear hidden price concessions and would see their payments itemized and shielded from retroactive clawbacks.

how_it_helps.text: For Medicare plans starting in 2026, PBMs and their affiliates could take no income from drug utilization other than bona fide service fees — flat-dollar, fair-market fees not based on drug price, rebates, or volume — with rebates and discounts from manufacturers allowed only if fully passed through to lower drug costs, and with enforcement through disgorgement of improper payments.

The bill bans spread pricing in Medicaid: payments to middlemen would be limited to actual ingredient cost plus a dispensing fee, passed through in full to the dispensing pharmacy, and any spread kept by the PBM would be disallowed for federal matching funds.

Plans would have to promptly tell each pharmacy how a claim was priced — fees, discounts, and price concessions included — in a standardized format, and could only use standardized, pharmacy-type-specific performance measures when adjusting pharmacy payments.

Plans could no longer restrict access to most drugs to a chosen subset of pharmacies, and would have to report what share of drugs is dispensed by pharmacies affiliated with the PBM and how plans steer patients into PBM-owned mail and specialty pharmacies.

PBMs would file detailed annual reports on what they retain per drug, what their affiliated pharmacies were paid versus independent ones, and any contracts tying one drug's rebate to coverage conditions on other drugs, with audits by the plan.

analysis.who_pays: The PBM industry and its corporate parents (including insurers that own PBMs), which would lose spread-pricing revenue and price-based fees in Medicare and Medicaid and face heavy new reporting and audit duties; taxpayers would fund roughly $35 million in administration and oversight appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Most of the information PBMs must report is treated as confidential: the Secretary is barred from publicly disclosing it in a way that identifies a specific PBM, plan, manufacturer, or contract prices, so the public would see only aggregate summaries rather than named companies and prices.

The bill leaves the manufacturer-rebate system intact: PBMs may keep receiving rebates calculated as a percentage of a drug's price as long as they pass them fully through to the plan, so much of the rebate-based pricing structure that critics say inflates list prices continues under this framework.

The changes impose substantial reporting, audit, and compliance obligations on PBMs and plans, with the cost of those obligations ultimately absorbed in program administration — and some analysts of PBM regulation have argued that restricting PBM compensation models could change negotiating arrangements in ways that are hard to predict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core changes — flat service fees instead of price-based pay, a Medicaid spread-pricing ban, and itemized payment transparency for pharmacies — attack documented ways middlemen capture money between the plan, the pharmacy, and the manufacturer, and they are the kinds of structural rules that persist once in place. The main weaknesses are that the resulting disclosures stay largely out of public view and the manufacturer rebate system itself is left standing, so the bill constrains PBM behavior more than it makes prices visible. On balance the benefits to beneficiaries and pharmacies appear larger than the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee reported the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar in December 2023, but no one brought it to the floor for a vote, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Wyden introduced the bill in the Senate on September 28, 2023, and it was referred to the Finance Committee, which he chairs.

On December 7, 2023, the Finance Committee reported the bill with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 266.
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never debated or voted on by the full Senate, and the House never took it up, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies keep the existing revenue model — spread pricing in Medicaid and price-based fees in Medicare — because no alternative passed; community pharmacies and beneficiaries continue under the current opaque payment arrangements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parents

for.name: Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; Chair, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, chaired the committee that reported it out with an amended substitute in December 2023.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute and written report No. 118-122 on December 7, 2023.

for.name: Independent community pharmacies
for.what_they_did: Publicly advocated for PBM payment and spread-pricing reforms as the businesses that bear below-cost reimbursements and retroactive fees.

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.role: Majority and Minority floor leaders, 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after it was placed on the calendar in December 2023, despite the bill sitting there for more than a year.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
against.role: Three companies processing the large majority of U.S. prescription claims
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against PBM legislation that would ban spread pricing and price-based fees, arguing middlemen negotiate savings for plans.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no roll-call record of partisan positions, though PBM regulation had vocal supporters in both parties throughout the Congress.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill bars PBMs and their affiliates from taking anything but flat, fair-market service fees in Medicare and outlaws spread pricing in Medicaid, eliminating revenue streams tied to drug prices. Their current fees are funded by the plans, pharmacies, and manufacturers whose money flows through the system, so their gain under the status quo is ordinary patients' cost.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers that own PBMs and pharmacies (CVS Health, Cigna, UnitedHealth)
industries.note: These parent companies would have to report what their affiliated pharmacies are paid versus independent ones, why branded drugs are favored over generics and biosimilars, and what they retain per drug, threatening the internal-margin strategy that links insurance, PBM, and pharmacy ownership.

Pharmacies would receive itemized claim-level pricing information, standardized performance measures instead of opaque fee clawbacks, a Medicaid spread-pricing ban, and limits on plans restricting drugs to a chosen subset of pharmacies — the practices community pharmacists say drive them below cost.

The bill leaves the rebate system intact and even permits price-percentage rebates if fully passed through, but requires PBMs to disclose contracts that tie one drug's rebate to coverage conditions on others and to justify covering brand drugs over available generics and biosimilars, adding pressure on brand-pricing strategies.

The programs would gain guardrails against middleman markups, at the cost of roughly $35 million in appropriations for CMS and HHS Inspector General oversight and a provision replenishing the Medicare Improvement Fund.
